Elham is a young, unmarried author — likely a Muslimah — who crossed over into the reality she had been writing about by Falling: a sleep-crossing in which both mind and body leave her original world entirely. She is not the first Author to have written of this realm, but her stories are among the most current accounts of it. The pressing difficulty of her situation is that humans are registered in this world as soon as they arrive, and while that registration is not always malevolent in intent, it functions like invasive surveillance — well-meaning paparazzi indifferent to privacy — meaning that concealing her identity as both a human and an Author is not optional. She knows that her worries are at least partly paranoia, but she also knows that one slip could unmask her. That exposure risk is precisely why she cannot simply leave: departing too quickly or calling attention to herself before she has established any cover would invite the very scrutiny she is trying to avoid. Early in the story she finds herself in the main antagonist's domain, and the central pressure of that section is navigating a way out without being caught.

The antagonist himself is described as something like the head of a mafia, but farther-reaching and reading less like a conventional crime boss and more like the Capricorn of Inkheart — his name is planned to carry the words "Silver" and "Heart" in some form, though not literally as "Silverheart." Critically, he is not without a soul; a softer side either once existed or still does, and this is precisely what makes Elham's position so precarious in his eyes. She did not earn that knowledge of his interior dimension through any trust he extended to her — she simply wrote it, which means she holds intimate understanding of him through no sanctioned means. He would be right to see that as a violation, and the notes make clear she could be viewed as a dangerous asset or a threat because of it. His right-hand man, the Sparrow, is the one who comes to take her somewhere she needs to go — and she recognizes him fully, having written a great deal of his story and knowing even what she hasn't yet set down on the page. The Sparrow, like his leader, is not irredeemably cruel; his method of recruitment is to treat people well and present them with a choice — stay and work for us, or eventually leave and fend for yourself — and earn loyalty that way rather than by force. Even the hero of her books, she has realized, may have cause to take issue with her, given how personally Authors tend to write about their characters.

— From your notes only. Nothing invented.
